x.ASV: For the Chief Musician; set to Al-tashheth. A Psalm of Asaph, a Song. We give thanks unto thee, O God; We give thanks, for thy name is near: Men tell of thy wondrous works.
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. 'Destroy not.' A Psalm of Asaph: a Song. Unto thee we give thanks, OGod, we give thanks; and thy name is near: thy marvellous works declare it.
x.KJV: To the chief Musician, Al–taschith, A Psalm or Song of Asaph. Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare.
x.YLT: To the Overseer. --`Destroy not.' --A Psalm of Asaph. --A Song. We have given thanks to Thee, O God, We have given thanks, and near is Thy name, They have recounted Thy wonders.

nt: The psalmist is repeating the phrase **We give thanks** in order to intensify the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [We thank you so very much]

By **your name is near**, the psalmist means that God is present and accessible to his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you are present with us] or [you are close to us]
The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent God himself and his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your presence]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [we your people recount]

x.ASV: When I shall find the set time, I will judge uprightly.
x.Darby: When I shall receive the assembly, I will judge with equity.
x.KJV: When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly.
x.YLT: When I receive an appointment, I--I do judge uprightly.

nt: כִּ֭י אֶקַּ֣ח מוֹעֵ֑ד אֲ֝נִ֗י מֵישָׁרִ֥ים אֶשְׁפֹּֽט

This is the beginning of what God said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of God. Alternate translation: [God said, “When I take the appointed time, I will judge with equity]

God is stating the pronoun **I** twice, even though the verb already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one speaking and acting. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [I myself will judge]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **equity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right] or [uprightly]

x.ASV: The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I have set up the pillars of it. [Selah
x.Darby: The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I have established its pillars. Selah.
x.KJV: The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah.
x.YLT: Melted is the earth and all its inhabitants, I--I have pondered its pillars. Selah.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of the earth and its inhabitants as if they were **melting**. He means that they are overcome with fear and instability in the presence of God’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The earth and all its inhabitants are trembling with fear]

God is stating the pronoun **I** explicitly, even though the verb already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who establishes the earth’s foundations. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [I myself established]

The psalmist is speaking of the earth as if it were a building with **pillars** to support it. This image represents the stability that God provides and maintains for the earth. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [made it stable] or [keep it stable]

x.ASV: I said unto the arrogant, Deal not arrogantly; And to the wicked, Lift not up the horn:
x.Darby: I said unto the boastful, Boast not; and to the wicked, Lift not up the horn:
x.KJV: I said unto the fools, Deal not foolishly: and to the wicked, Lift not up the horn:
x.YLT: I have said to the boastful, `Be not boastful,' And to the wicked, `Raise not up a horn.'

nt: David is using the adjective **boasters** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who boast]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

The psalmist is speaking of arrogant or defiant people as if they were to physically **lift up a horn** like an animal displaying strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [behave arrogantly] or [act defiantly]

x.ASV: Lift not up your horn on high; Speak not with a stiff neck.
x.Darby: Lift not up your horn on high; speak not arrogantly with a [stiff] neck.
x.KJV: Lift not up your horn on high: speak not with a stiff neck.
x.YLT: Raise not up on high your horn, (Ye speak with a stiff neck.)

nt: The psalmist is speaking of **to the height** as if it were a physical elevation to which one could **lift up** a **horn**. This intensifies the image of arrogance that the horn metaphor conveys. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [act with extreme arrogance]

Here, **neck** represents speaking with an arrogant attitude. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [speak arrogantly]

x.ASV: For neither from the east, nor from the west, Nor yet from the south, cometh lifting up.
x.Darby: For not from the east nor from the west, nor yet from the south doth exaltation [come]:
x.KJV: For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south.
x.YLT: For not from the east, or from the west, Nor from the wilderness-- is elevation.

nt: The psalmist is referring to all directions on earth by naming two (or three) cardinal points, **the east**, **the west**, and **the wilderness** (the south). The word translated **comes lifting up** could possibly mean “mountains” which would refer to the north. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from any direction comes lifting up]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lifting up**, you could express the same idea with a verb such as “lift” or “exalt.” Alternate translation: [to lift someone up]

x.ASV: But God is the judge: He putteth down one, and lifteth up another.
x.Darby: ForGod is the judge; he putteth down one and exalteth another.
x.KJV: But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.
x.YLT: But God is judge, This He maketh low--and this He lifteth up.

nt: The implication is that God brings low the proud and wicked, and lifts up the humble and righteous. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he humbles this proud person, and he exalts this humble person] or [he brings down the arrogant, and he raises up the lowly]

x.ASV: For in the hand of Jehovah there is a cup, and the wine foameth; It is full of mixture, and he poureth out of the same: Surely the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall drain them, and drink them.
x.Darby: For in the hand of Jehovah there is a cup, and it foameth with wine, it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same; yea, the dregs thereof shall all the wicked of the earth drain off, [and] drink.
x.KJV: For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.
x.YLT: For a cup is in the hand of Jehovah, And the wine hath foamed, It is full of mixture, and He poureth out of it, Only its dregs wring out, and drink, Do all the wicked of the earth,

nt: The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s judgment as if it were **a cup** that Yahweh held **in** his **hand** and forced people to drink. This is a common biblical image. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s judgment is like a cup in his hand]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **wine** that **foams** and is **a full mixture** refers to wine mixed with spices, making it very strong and intoxicating, representing the full strength of God’s judgment. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the wine foams, full of spices]

The psalmist is speaking of punishment as if it were a cup of wine and God’s enemies **will drain** even **its dregs**, the sediment at the bottom. He means that they will experience God’s judgment completely, even to its most severe and bitter aspects. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will experience the punishment fully, even its worst parts]
See how you translated the similar expression in [verse 4](../075/004.md).

nt: וַ֭⁠אֲנִי אַגִּ֣יד לְ⁠עֹלָ֑ם אֲ֝זַמְּרָ֗ה לֵ⁠אלֹהֵ֥י יַעֲקֹֽב

This is the beginning of what the psalmist said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of the psalmist. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I will declare to eternity; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** twice for emphasis. He is doing that to emphasize his personal commitment and determination, in contrast to the wicked. If a speaker of your language would repeat a pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I will declare]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel, the descendants of Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the God of the people of Israel] or [to the God of the Israelites]

x.Darby: And all the horns of the wicked will I cut off; [but] the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.
x.KJV: All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.

nt: וְ⁠כָל־קַרְנֵ֣י רְשָׁעִ֣ים אֲגַדֵּ֑עַ תְּ֝רוֹמַ֗מְנָה קַֽרְנ֥וֹת צַדִּֽיק

This is the beginning of what God said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of God. Alternate translation: [God says, “And all the horns of the wicked I will cut off; the horns of the righteous will be lifted up.”]

The psalmist is speaking of power and strength as if they were **horns**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of the wicked … the power of the righteous]
See how you translated the similar expression in [verse 4](../075/004.md).

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

The expression **will be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [I will lift up] or [God will lift up]
